article_title: Chapter One (Formerly Innovations for Learning High Impact Tutoring)
citation: Chapter One. (2024). Chapter One — Evidence Rating: Strong. https://www.evidenceforlearning.org/chapter-one
title: Push-in short-burst tutoring with personalized dosage
description: The program's instructional pattern places tutors inside the regular classroom rather than pulling students out: tutors "work with individual students in 5-10 minute increment sessions during blocks of reading instruction or other opportune moments." Session length and frequency vary by student need and rate of progress, with students needing more support meeting daily for periods of time. A student-relay handoff minimizes interruptions to classroom instruction.
requirements: Part-time tutors embedded in the classroom who serve multiple classrooms across the school
target_learners: kindergarten and first grade students needing supplementary reading support
target_learning_goals: phonics
reading fluency
examples: Students making adequate progress meet with their tutor once or twice a week, whereas students identified as needing more support may meet daily for periods of time
key_sources: Chapter One. (2024). Chapter One — Evidence Rating: Strong. https://www.evidenceforlearning.org/chapter-one

article_title: The impact of a technology-enhanced math performance task on student cognitive engagement in mathematics
citation: Meg Guerreiro. (2017). The impact of a technology-enhanced math performance task on student cognitive engagement in mathematics. NWEA Research white paper. https://www.nwea.org
title: Technological affordances in assessments should be purposefully implemented; simply putting tests on computers may not be enough
description: The article's design recommendation is that technology in assessment should be implemented deliberately for its affordances rather than applied as a default conversion of tests to computer delivery. It states that "just putting tests on computers may not be enough and technological affordance should be purposefully implemented." This follows from the null platform effect on cognitive engagement combined with student appreciation of specific interactive features.
requirements: A purpose for each technological affordance, such as the interactivity and animations students cited as helping them visualize and work through problems
constraints: The between-subjects ANOVA found no relationship between platform modality and cognitive engagement, so platform choice alone did not change measured engagement
target_learning_goals: cognitive engagement during mathematics assessment
examples: The study compared technology-enhanced (animation and interactivity), technology-enabled (computer-based without animation and interactivity), and paper-and-pencil platforms on the same mathematics performance task
key_sources: Meg Guerreiro. (2017). The impact of a technology-enhanced math performance task on student cognitive engagement in mathematics. NWEA Research white paper. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/the-impact-of-a-technology-enhanced-math-performance-task-on-student-cognitive-engagement-in-mathematics/

article_title: Providing Reading Interventions for Students in Grades 4–9
citation: Vaughn, S., Gersten, R., Dimino, J., Taylor, M. J., Newman-Gonchar, R., Krowka, S., Kieffer, M. J., McKeown, M., Reed, D., Sanchez, M., St. Martin, K., Wexler, J., Morgan, S., Yañez, A., & Jayanthi, M. (2022). Providing Reading Interventions for Students in Grades 4–9 (WWC 2022007). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance (NCEE), Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://whatworks.ed.gov/
title: Give each repeated reading a purpose rather than rereading only for speed
description: Rereading the same passage several times builds fluency, but unstructured rereading can feel dull and discouraging for upper-elementary and middle school students. The guide recommends that "students reread the same passage a total of 3–4 times, each time with a different purpose," such as answering questions, identifying unknown words, or reading with expression, and that teachers briefly discuss responses after each reading to hold students accountable. Purposes can vary with the reading ability of the group.
requirements: Choose short, content-rich passages at students' instructional level that include previously taught words, sounds, or vocabulary
Provide feedback after each reading that affirms correct responses and clarifies misconceptions
constraints: Timed readings should be used with caution because they can be overused and can detrimentally affect engagement and motivation when used solely to increase speed
target_learners: Students in grades 4-9 with reading difficulties
target_learning_goals: Reading text effortlessly and with understanding
examples: Example 2.2 shows a small group reading a paragraph on poverty and feeding a family, first silently explaining it to a partner, then reading aloud in turns to answer board questions
key_sources: Vaughn, S., Gersten, R., Dimino, J., Taylor, M. J., Newman-Gonchar, R., Krowka, S., Kieffer, M. J., McKeown, M., Reed, D., Sanchez, M., St. Martin, K., Wexler, J., Morgan, S., Yañez, A., & Jayanthi, M. (2022). Providing Reading Interventions for Students in Grades 4–9 (WWC 2022007). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance (NCEE), Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/29

article_title: Paradise Unified School District: "Building School Mental Health Systems to Support Healing and Recovery through Project Cal-Well"
citation: Paradise Unified School District: Building School Mental Health Systems to Support Healing and Recovery Through Project Cal-Well. (2024). WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Universal mental health screening toolkit: SAEBRS, SDQ, ProQOL, and monthly Kelvin real-time pulses
description: PUSD implemented universal mental health screeners starting in 2019/20, including the Social, Academic, & Emotional Behavior Risk Screener (SAEBRS), the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ), and the Professional Quality of Life (ProQOL) measure. In 2023/24 the district advanced this approach "by integrating data from monthly Kelvin real-time pulses," which allow "site administrators to customize monthly questions based on their specific goals." Screening and data use is one of the district's Tier 1 priorities.
requirements: administration beginning in 2019/20 and data integration processes for site administrators
constraints: ProQOL is a Professional Quality of Life measure, i.e., aimed at staff quality of life rather than students, as cited by the brief
target_learners: PUSD students in grades served by the screeners, plus staff via ProQOL
target_learning_goals: identifying social, academic, and emotional behavior risk; monitoring student and staff well-being for data-informed support
examples: monthly Kelvin pulses customized by site administrators to their specific goals in 2023/24
key_sources: Paradise Unified School District: Building School Mental Health Systems to Support Healing and Recovery Through Project Cal-Well. (2024). WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655970

article_title: Paradise Unified School District: "Building School Mental Health Systems to Support Healing and Recovery through Project Cal-Well"
citation: Paradise Unified School District: Building School Mental Health Systems to Support Healing and Recovery Through Project Cal-Well. (2024). WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Grant-funded school-based Wellness Centers as accessible hubs for services
description: With Project Cal-Well support, PUSD established grant-funded Wellness Centers in partnership with Butte County Behavioral Health, first at Paradise High School in 2021/22, then Ridgeview High School in 2022/23, and Paradise Junior High School in 2024/25. They "serve as accessible hubs for essential services, including mental health supports and access to community aid (e.g., food, housing support)." The district plans additional sites and commits to Wellness Centers on every school campus.
requirements: grant funding and partnership with Butte County Behavioral Health
constraints: initially launched only at high school and junior high sites, with districtwide expansion still planned
target_learners: secondary students at PUSD school sites
target_learning_goals: access to mental health supports and community aid that remove barriers to well-being and school participation
examples: Paradise High School 2021/22, Ridgeview High School 2022/23, Paradise Junior High School 2024/25 launches

article_title: Using AI in engineering education: a balancing act, driven by clear purpose
citation: Kudina, O. (2025). Using AI in engineering education: a balancing act, driven by clear purpose. Draft version, to appear in The Routledge Handbook of the Philosophy of Engineering, 2nd ed.
title: Adopt AI in education only in a purpose-driven, context-sensitive way, weighing pedagogical benefits against known risks including environmental costs
description: The chapter proposes that "Any potential adoption of AI in education should be purpose-driven": educators clarify why GenAI is needed in a course or assignment, what added value it represents, and how it contributes to learning objectives, then assess controlled experimentation against that initial motivation. If evidence does not support the intentions, educators should object to AI use for that purpose, positioning pedagogical benefits against known risks, including environmental and water costs of GenAI.
requirements: Educators clarify purpose via questions such as what added value the technology represents for the learning objectives
Controlled experimentation assessed for evidence against the initial motivation
constraints: In cases of doubt or no clearly supported purpose, the author urges erring on the side of caution and not using GenAI
target_learning_goals: alignment of AI use with learning objectives
sustainability awareness in technology choices
examples: The author cites the UNESCO report figure that ChatGPT's roughly 1 billion daily queries add up to roughly 310 GWh per year, urging educators to keep such environmental costs in view
key_sources: Kudina, O. (2025). Using AI in engineering education: a balancing act, driven by clear purpose. Draft version, to appear in The Routledge Handbook of the Philosophy of Engineering, 2nd ed. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16626

article_title: PromptDecipher: Supporting AI Tutor Authoring Through Editable Simulated Interactions
citation: Miina Koyama, Ruiwei Xiao, and John Stamper. (2026). PromptDecipher: Supporting AI Tutor Authoring Through Editable Simulated Interactions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16605
title: Structurally embedded quality assurance: publication gated behind completed test-correct-verify cycles
description: This pattern embeds quality assurance structurally in the authoring workflow rather than relying on voluntary compliance. Publication is blocked until all test cases are marked as passed, and "publication is gated behind at least one completed cycle" of testing, correcting, and verification. The article states this "enforces QA as a first-class activity and scaffolds teachers in roles they would otherwise skip," addressing the finding that teachers rarely test bots before deployment.
requirements: A suite of pre-defined test scenarios with simulated student profiles, and a mechanism that blocks publication until test cases pass
constraints: The article reports the pattern as designed and demonstrated; whether it increases testing rates at scale is a planned future analysis
target_learners: teachers and higher-education instructors authoring AI tutors
target_learning_goals: systematic pre-deployment testing of AI tutoring chatbots
examples: In the PromptDecipher workflow, a teacher clicks 'Mark pass' to approve each test case, and once all cases pass the bot goes live with a shareable link.
key_sources: Miina Koyama, Ruiwei Xiao, and John Stamper. (2026). PromptDecipher: Supporting AI Tutor Authoring Through Editable Simulated Interactions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16605
grain_size: workflow-level design pattern for authoring tools

article_title: Pulla: A Parsons Problem Tool for Fine-Grained Behavioral Tracing and Instructor-Facing Problem-Solving Analysis
citation: Daniel Prol, Juho Leinonen, Arto Hellas, Saleh Alkhamees, Amin Alipour. (2026). Pulla: A Parsons Problem Tool for Fine-Grained Behavioral Tracing and Instructor-Facing Problem-Solving Analysis. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15944
title: Pulla: a Parsons problem tool with client-side behavioral tracing, an instructor dashboard, and on-demand AI difficulty analysis
description: Pulla extends CodeCheck, an open-source web-based programming assessment platform, with "a behavioral instrumentation layer designed to capture students' problem-solving processes while working on Parsons problems". It records six interaction event types (e.g., parsons_tile_click, parsons_erase, check_submit, parsons_guess) plus submission snapshots with per-block green/yellow/red feedback, persisted to PostgreSQL. An instructor dashboard shows per-student attempt histories and activity logs, and an on-demand GPT-4.1-mini pipeline produces labeled per-student difficulty reports and class-level PowerPoint summary slides. Blocks are auto-indented on placement, avoiding misindentation difficulty documented in prior work.
requirements: Instructors must explicitly invoke the AI analysis; it runs on-demand from the Student Profile View or submissions page
Students access problems through a link in the course LMS
constraints: The dashboard's value depends on instructor engagement, per the authors' stated limitations
target_learners: CS majors in an upper-division software design course
non-CS majors in an introductory programming course
target_learning_goals: exception handling concepts, including selecting semantically appropriate exception types and raising versus silently returning
examples: Deployed in a Java software design course at the University of Houston (68 students, Spring 2026) and an online self-paced Python CS1 course at Aalto University (36 students, Summer 2026), in graded assignments
key_sources: Daniel Prol, Juho Leinonen, Arto Hellas, Saleh Alkhamees, Amin Alipour. (2026). Pulla: A Parsons Problem Tool for Fine-Grained Behavioral Tracing and Instructor-Facing Problem-Solving Analysis. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15944

article_title: Purpose Before Policy: Academic Integrity, Generative AI, and Rhetorical Stance
citation: Tristan B. Taylor & Travis LaCroix. (2026). Purpose before policy: academic integrity, generative AI, and rhetorical stance. Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-026-01706-1
title: Ensure coherence between stated missions, pedagogical practices, and technology approaches before enforcing academic integrity standards on students
description: The article's central design recommendation for institutions: universities "cannot credibly enforce integrity standards in the age of AI without first ensuring coherence between their stated missions, pedagogical practices, and approaches to emerging technologies". Because integrity functions as a social contract, institutions must first uphold their own obligations to clarity, coherence, and educational purpose; misaligned curricula and policies that individualise responsibility undermine institutional credibility. The principle addresses systemic conditions rather than student character.
requirements: Institutions must clearly articulate their educational goals and communicate the function and purpose of higher education to stakeholders before holding students accountable
constraints: The authors note universities operate through fragmented, localised practices varying across faculties, departments, and classrooms, and that GenAI exposes misalignments rather than creating them
target_learning_goals: academic integrity
coherent institutional policy and pedagogy around emerging technologies
examples: The article contrasts institutions with contradictory stances (endorsing AI tools while policing their use) with the argument that policy contradictions produce moral double binds that incentivise misconduct.
key_sources: Tristan B. Taylor & Travis LaCroix. (2026). Purpose before policy: academic integrity, generative AI, and rhetorical stance. Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-026-01706-1

article_title: Beyond Detection: Redesigning Authentic Assessment in an AI-Mediated World
citation: Kickbusch, S., Ashford-Rowe, K., Kemp, A., Boreland, J., & Huijser, H. (2025). Beyond Detection: Redesigning Authentic Assessment in an AI-Mediated World. Education Sciences, 15(11), 1537. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci15111537
title: Design tasks where tool use is purposeful and aligned with intended learning outcomes
description: The paper states the embedding principle is "not simply “include the tools students might use” but rather “design tasks where tool use is purposeful and aligned with intended learning outcomes.”" Assessment focus shifts to how students curate their use of technologies rather than whether they can replicate outputs GenAI already provides. Digital tools should support, not substitute, higher-order capabilities such as critical reasoning and ethical judgement.
requirements: Assessment criteria must emphasise judgement, ethics and decision quality rather than tool mechanics
constraints: Tasks that ban AI use risk constructing artificial forms of assessment divorced from professional reality
target_learners: higher education students in technology-rich disciplines
target_learning_goals: critical engagement with digital tools
professional judgement and adaptability
examples: A journalism assessment requires students to critique and edit an AI-generated news brief to assess bias identification and ethical reporting standards
key_sources: Kickbusch, S., Ashford-Rowe, K., Kemp, A., Boreland, J., & Huijser, H. (2025). Beyond Detection: Redesigning Authentic Assessment in an AI-Mediated World. Education Sciences, 15(11), 1537. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci15111537

article_title: Purposely Teaching for the Promotion of Higher-order Thinking Skills: A Case of Critical Thinking
citation: Miri, B., David, BC. & Uri, Z. (2007). Purposely Teaching for the Promotion of Higher-order Thinking Skills: A Case of Critical Thinking. Res Sci Educ 37, 353–369. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11165-006-9029-2
title: Teach higher order thinking purposely and persistently to develop students' critical thinking capabilities
description: The article's central design recommendation is that teachers should "purposely and persistently practice higher order thinking strategies" rather than relying on traditional instruction, because the study found significant critical thinking gains only in the group so taught. It presents this as giving "a good chance for a consequent development of critical thinking capabilities". The principle applies within science education classrooms where teachers deliberately plan for thinking skills.
requirements: Teachers must deliberately plan and persistently enact higher order thinking strategies over time, not teach traditionally
constraints: Evidence base is a longitudinal case study within science education; the article states a good chance of development, not a guaranteed outcome
target_learning_goals: critical thinking skills
disposition towards critical thinking
examples: An experimental group of 57 science students exposed to higher order thinking teaching strategies showed significant critical thinking improvement while traditionally taught controls did not
key_sources: Miri, B., David, BC. & Uri, Z. (2007). Purposely Teaching for the Promotion of Higher-order Thinking Skills: A Case of Critical Thinking. Res Sci Educ 37, 353–369. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11165-006-9029-2

article_title: Play it safe or play to learn: mindsets and behavioral self-regulation in kindergarten
citation: Compagnoni, M., Karlen, Y., & Maag Merki, K. (2019). Play it safe or play to learn: mindsets and behavioral self-regulation in kindergarten. Metacognition and Learning, 14, 291–314. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-019-09190-y
title: Puppet-and-touchscreen mindset scale for kindergarteners
description: A newly developed self-report mindset measure for kindergarteners based on the Berkeley Puppet Interview, with a goal-orientation scale (3 items) and a trait-belief scale (4 items). Two plush elephant puppets deliver standardized recorded answers on a touchscreen, and children indicate identification on a 5-point semantic differential scale with a "double binary response strategy" to counter endpoint pushing. The authors note the tool was "motivating for the children, easy to administer" and offers objectivity advantages.
requirements: Multiple-item scales are necessary with young children to ensure reliability, rather than single items
Children must be able to listen to and comprehend the recorded puppet statements; recorded statements can be replayed at the push of a button in case of comprehension problems
constraints: The trait beliefs scale showed low reliability in young children (α = .51), deemed sufficient for new scales and latent modeling
Mindset item distributions were left-skewed even after log transformation, with more children endorsing growth-oriented responses
target_learning_goals: assessing young children's motivational beliefs about trait stability and mastery versus performance goal orientations
examples: Administered individually in a roughly 25-minute session to 147 Swiss kindergarteners across two visits in spring 2017, with items based on the composite measure used by Gunderson et al. (2013) for children aged 7–8 years
key_sources: Compagnoni, M., Karlen, Y., & Maag Merki, K. (2019). Play it safe or play to learn: mindsets and behavioral self-regulation in kindergarten. Metacognition and Learning, 14, 291–314. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-019-09190-y

article_title: Novel CSCL design processes prompted by exploration of role-playing and emotions
citation: Sanna Järvelä · Carolyn P. Rosé. (2022). Novel CSCL design processes prompted by exploration of role-playing and emotions. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 17:457–461. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09383-9
title: Combined tangible puppets and 3D manipulable animations as perspective-taking manipulatives for CSCL role-play
description: The element combines "tangible puppets as mediating manipulates and 3D manipulable animations as perspective-taking manipulatives for role-playing in CSCL". It supports microteaching simulation for pre-service teachers, where the puppets mediate performance and the 3D animations let the teacher take the perspective of imaginary students, including nonverbal representations of characters. The editors call the nonverbal representations a possible key factor in dialogic thinking and performance.
requirements: Combination of both manipulative types (mediating and perspective-taking)
constraints: The editors note the key factor was the nonverbal representations of characters in the manipulatives
target_learners: pre-service student teachers in microteaching professional development
target_learning_goals: dialogic teaching skills and perspective-taking of imaginary students
examples: Student teacher microteaching role-plays with puppetry and 3D animations, analyzed with epistemic network analysis
key_sources: Sanna Järvelä · Carolyn P. Rosé. (2022). Novel CSCL design processes prompted by exploration of role-playing and emotions. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 17:457–461. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09383-9

article_title: A short teacher-led intervention using direct instruction enhances 5th graders' purposeful reading skills
citation: Potocki, A., Ayroles, J., & Rouet, J.-F. (2023). A short teacher-led intervention using direct instruction enhances 5th graders' purposeful reading skills. Learning and Instruction, 86, 101781. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101781
title: Five-module direct instruction program for purposeful reading strategies
description: The Purposeful Reading Training Program comprised five modules, each with two 45-minute workshops pairing a student workbook and a teacher guide. Each workshop followed explicit instruction phases: "presentation of the learning objective", "modelling", "guided practice" in pairs with corrective feedback, "individual practice", and a final "objectification phase" in which students make explicit the essential skills and knowledge to be retained. The first four modules targeted the MD-TRACE steps and the last coordinated them.
requirements: Teachers received a one-day training session and materials ahead of time, with ongoing researcher-teacher communication during implementation
constraints: Some teachers reported the workshops were sometimes too dense and difficult to carry out in 45 minutes only
target_learning_goals: declarative and procedural knowledge of purposeful reading strategies: question analysis, using textual cues, extracting and integrating information, constructing and checking answers
examples: Module tasks included underlining question keywords, choosing titles where answers were likely found, and assessing proposed answers for relevance and sufficiency
key_sources: Potocki, A., Ayroles, J., & Rouet, J.-F. (2023). A short teacher-led intervention using direct instruction enhances 5th graders' purposeful reading skills. Learning and Instruction, 86, 101781. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101781

article_title: The control of movement gradually transitions from feedback control to feedforward adaptation throughout childhood
citation: Malone, L. A., Hill, N. M., Tripp, H., Zipunnikov, V., Wolpert, D. M. & Bastian, A. J. (2025). The control of movement gradually transitions from feedback control to feedforward adaptation throughout childhood. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00304-7
title: Percentile reference curves for motor adaptation and overall performance in children aged 3–17
description: The article established smooth percentile curves (1st through 99th percentiles) for the mean initial angle (adaptation) and mean final angle (overall performance) at the end of learning, for the whole sample and by sex, from Push ball data of children aged 3–17. The article states these "are designed to be used as a reference, indicating how a child performed compared to other children aged 3–17 years on the Push ball task". The adaptation measure "increased gradually across age for the overall group, with males and females showing similar patterns".
requirements: Requires the remote Push ball visuomotor rotation task data from a large cross-sectional sample of children aged 3–17
constraints: The article states the reference percentile curves "should not yet be used as standards, adding value judgements and detailing how a child should adapt and perform"
target_learning_goals: Motor adaptation and sensorimotor learning development
examples: Supplementary Fig. 10 compares two 4-year-olds and two 10-year-olds showing different individual patterns of adaptation and overall performance relative to age-matched percentiles
key_sources: Malone, L. A., Hill, N. M., Tripp, H., Zipunnikov, V., Wolpert, D. M. & Bastian, A. J. (2025). The control of movement gradually transitions from feedback control to feedforward adaptation throughout childhood. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00304-7

article_title: An Interview Reflection on “Intelligent Tutoring Goes to School in the Big City”
citation: Kenneth R. Koedinger & Vincent Aleven. (2016). An Interview Reflection on “Intelligent Tutoring Goes to School in the Big City”. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 26, 13–24. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0082-8
title: PUMP Algebra Cognitive Tutor curriculum with embedded intelligent tutoring system
description: The PUMP (Pittsburgh Urban Mathematics Project) Algebra curriculum embedded the Algebra Cognitive Tutor into a complete redesigned course. The authors “would redesign the whole course from the bottom up including replacements for the textbook, new kinds of assessments, use of collaborative learning in the classroom portion of the curriculum, and new teaching approaches.” The recommended structure was non-technology text materials and classroom practices for 3 days a week and tutor use in the computer lab the other 2 days a week. It was evaluated in the 1993–94 school year in three city schools with a high proportion of low income and low performing students.
requirements: Integration of the tutor technology with other teaching practices and the existing social context of schools
constraints: In the first study there was not quite enough tutor material to reach the 3-day classroom / 2-day lab goal
target_learners: high-school algebra students, including a high proportion of low income and low performing students
target_learning_goals: practical and general understanding of algebra
examples: Recommended use of non-technology text materials and classroom practices 3 days a week and tutor use in the computer lab 2 days a week
key_sources: Kenneth R. Koedinger & Vincent Aleven. (2016). An Interview Reflection on “Intelligent Tutoring Goes to School in the Big City”. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 26, 13–24. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0082-8

article_title: Factors contributing to teachers’ acceptance intention to gamified EFL tools: a scale development study
citation: Zhanni Luo. (2024). Factors contributing to teachers' acceptance intention to gamified EFL tools: a scale development study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10249-6
title: PU-gamification-EFL and PEoU-gamification-EFL scales
description: Two validated survey instruments measuring secondary school teachers' perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use of gamified EFL tools, developed through expert interviews, 347 email interviews, 14 face-to-face interviews, and a 512-teacher survey. The final PU scale contains five items and the PEoU scale six items, all on a 7-point Likert format. The article reports the PU scale reached "the value of the internal consistency of 0.899" and both constructs showed AVE above the 0.5 cut-off criterion.
requirements: Administered as 7-point Likert items; items were context-customised for gamified EFL teaching in secondary schools
constraints: Validated in the context of gamified EFL tools in Chinese secondary schools; the article notes findings might not be limited to test-oriented educational contexts
target_learning_goals: measuring perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use of gamified EFL tools
examples: PU items include relatedness items adapted from Venkatesh and Davis (2000) and engagement items drafted from interview responses
key_sources: Zhanni Luo. (2024). Factors contributing to teachers' acceptance intention to gamified EFL tools: a scale development study. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10249-6

article_title: The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic
citation: van Niekerk, J.F. (2015). The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic. Nelson Mandela Metropolitan University.
title: Purpose-designed qualitative instrument organised around six experience themes
description: The study used a purpose-designed qualitative research instrument (Appendix A) whose thematic organisation is summarised in Table 3.1. The results chapter analyses six themes: whether the e-learning material differed from "normal" classes, whether it was engaging (enjoyable), whether students preferred it, whether learning was a positive experience, whether the material was "rich" enough (multimedia), and whether students felt they had learned. Closed-question responses are reported in Tables 4.4-4.9 and Figures 4.1-4.12, plus open-ended questions.
requirements: Used alongside quantitative analysis of formal assessments in a mixed-methods pragmatic design
target_learners: Technical Programming 1 students using the e-learning intervention
target_learning_goals: student motivation to learn and experience of the e-learning environment
key_sources: van Niekerk, J.F. (2015). The effectiveness of brain-compatible blended learning material in the teaching of programming logic. Nelson Mandela Metropolitan University. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2016.09.008

article_title: What Is the Minimum Information Needed to Estimate Average Treatment Effects in Education RCTs?
citation: Schochet, Peter Z. (2013). What is the Minimum Information Needed to Estimate Average Treatment Effects in Education RCTs? SREE Spring 2013 Conference Abstract. http://www.whitehouse.gov/sites/default/files/omb/memoranda/2013/m-13-17.pdf
title: Demonstration set of published education RCTs funded by IES, the Department of Labor, and foundations
description: The article plans to demonstrate the proposed estimation methods using several published RCTs. As printed: "These RCTs tested the effects of a wide range of education interventions, including early elementary school math curricula, , selected reading comprehension interventions, Teach for America, and Job Corps." Random assignment was at the student, school, or teacher (classroom) level in low-performing school districts, with math or reading test scores of elementary students as key outcomes for most studies.
requirements: RCT designs spanning student-level, school-level, and classroom-level randomization to exercise the full range of estimators
constraints: Demonstrations use existing published RCTs rather than new data collection
target_learners: Elementary school students in low-performing school districts; Job Corps participants
target_learning_goals: Estimating effects of math and reading interventions on achievement test scores
examples: Interventions named in the abstract include early elementary school math curricula, selected reading comprehension interventions, Teach for America, and Job Corps
key_sources: Schochet, Peter Z. (2013). What is the Minimum Information Needed to Estimate Average Treatment Effects in Education RCTs? SREE Spring 2013 Conference Abstract. http://www.whitehouse.gov/sites/default/files/omb/memoranda/2013/m-13-17.pdf

article_title: Effect of Power Point Enhanced Teaching (Visual Input) on Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners' Listening Comprehension Ability
citation: Samira Sehati, Morteza Khodabandehlou. (2017). Effect of Power Point Enhanced Teaching (Visual Input) on Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners' Listening Comprehension Ability. Journal of Educational Issues, Vol. 3, No. 2. https://doi.org/10.5296/jei.v3i2.12323
title: Use technology in listening instruction purposefully to increase learning, not for the sake of using it
description: In its conclusion the article advises that teachers use PowerPoint "smartly and wisely to assist their teaching", vary their methods according to students' needs and interests, and use technology-assisted teaching more intensively and frequently. It stresses that "educators should not use technology in the classroom just for the sake of using it"; instead, educators should develop innovative teaching strategies that increase student learning and comprehension of listening, adopting technology only when it helps achieve that goal.
requirements: Teachers should consider carefully whether technology-assisted teaching is more effective than the traditional listening method for their students
constraints: The article's recommendation is grounded in the authors' belief and the study's positive result, not in a comparison of technology conditions
target_learning_goals: listening comprehension ability
student learning and comprehension of listening skill
examples: The study's experimental group received PowerPoint-enhanced listening teaching over eight sessions and outperformed the traditionally taught control group on the post-test
key_sources: Samira Sehati, Morteza Khodabandehlou. (2017). Effect of Power Point Enhanced Teaching (Visual Input) on Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners' Listening Comprehension Ability. Journal of Educational Issues, Vol. 3, No. 2. https://doi.org/10.5296/jei.v3i2.12323

article_title: Formation of the Professional and Didactic Culture of the Future Teacher
citation: Mirzagitova, A. L. & Akhmetov, L. G. (2016). Formation of the Professional and Didactic Culture of the Future Teacher. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(14), 6675-6689. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1118411
title: Interconnected chain purpose-means-result at standard and individual levels
description: The article recommends using two levels of the interconnected chain purpose-means-result in preparing future teachers. The first, standard, level evaluates the quality of the compulsory minimum of subject assimilation using regular assessment standards; the second, individual, level evaluates the quality of the individual development of the student using individual assessment standards and the intensity of the personality development.
requirements: The article states the standard level has traditionally been used in the pedagogical process.
target_learning_goals: individual professional development
assessment of personality development
examples: The individual level allows determination of the progress in the individual professional development of each student.
key_sources: Mirzagitova, A. L. & Akhmetov, L. G. (2016). Formation of the Professional and Didactic Culture of the Future Teacher. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(14), 6675-6689. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1115889

article_title: Active learning-based reinforcement in nursing education: a cluster-randomized controlled trial using Roper, Logan and Tierney's life model.
citation: Eren Nadiye Barış; Çiftçi Bahar. (2026). Active learning–based reinforcement in nursing education: a cluster-randomized controlled trial using Roper, Logan and Tierney's life model. Revista da Escola de Enfermagem da USP. https://doi.org/10.1590/1980-220X-REEUSP-2026-0022en
title: Puzzle Booklet: a 10-sheet, multi-format puzzle reinforcement tool for the Roper, Logan and Tierney Life Model
description: The Puzzle Booklet is an instructional reinforcement tool built from an item pool of approximately 200 questions, from which 100 items were selected into "a booklet containing 10 puzzle sheets, with approximately 10 items per sheet". Formats included matching, word search, crossword, and clinical case-based items created with an online puzzle generator. Five faculty experts reviewed it for content validity; it was completed individually during class and as follow-up assignments over one week.
requirements: Alignment with course learning objectives and expert review by five faculty experts
Completion individually during class time and as follow-up assignments, with instructor monitoring and feedback
constraints: Used as an instructional reinforcement tool rather than an outcome measure, so formal psychometric testing was not conducted
Designed explicitly for first-year students, with attention to balancing cognitive load
target_learning_goals: Recall of Roper, Logan and Tierney's Life Model content
Critical thinking, problem-solving, and application of theoretical knowledge to clinical practice
examples: In crossword activities students defined key life activities such as elimination or communication; in matching activities they paired interventions with corresponding life activities
key_sources: Eren Nadiye Barış; Çiftçi Bahar. (2026). Active learning–based reinforcement in nursing education: a cluster-randomized controlled trial using Roper, Logan and Tierney's life model. Revista da Escola de Enfermagem da USP. https://doi.org/10.1590/1980-220X-REEUSP-2026-0022en

article_title: Active learning-based reinforcement in nursing education: a cluster-randomized controlled trial using Roper, Logan and Tierney's life model.
citation: Eren Nadiye Barış; Çiftçi Bahar. (2026). Active learning–based reinforcement in nursing education: a cluster-randomized controlled trial using Roper, Logan and Tierney's life model. Revista da Escola de Enfermagem da USP. https://doi.org/10.1590/1980-220X-REEUSP-2026-0022en
title: Puzzle-based learning as an active-learning strategy grounded in constructivist learning theory
description: The article frames puzzle-based learning as aligning with "the principles of active learning" and constructivist learning theory, which emphasizes that learners construct understanding through engagement and problem-solving. Puzzles are said to encourage cognitive processing, critical thinking, and knowledge retention by requiring students to connect concepts, fostering deeper learning through active involvement rather than passive reception. The trial applies this framing by using puzzles as reinforcement after an interactive lecture.
requirements: Puzzles designed to align with learning objectives and balanced cognitive demands
Integration into the course flow as a formative learning tool
constraints: Evidence of effectiveness in teaching comprehensive nursing care models such as the Life Model remains limited, per the authors
target_learning_goals: Knowledge retention
Motivation toward instructional materials
Critical thinking

article_title: Game-based blended learning versus traditional lecture for evidence-based medicine (EBM) competencies in undergraduate medical students: a quasi-experimental study.
citation: Zand Vahid, Bazi Ramin, Keshmiri Fatemeh. (2026). Game-based blended learning versus traditional lecture for evidence-based medicine (EBM) competencies in undergraduate medical students: a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09628-3
title: Puzzle-based card-sorting and sequencing activities organizing the sequential EBM decision-making pathway
description: The intervention used puzzle materials designed as "card-sorting and sequencing activities rather than interlocking physical puzzle pieces", requiring students to match and organize shuffled cards into the correct logical sequence corresponding to each clinical scenario. Twelve puzzle sets were developed, each containing four clinical scenarios and seven EBM-related component categories, resulting in 28 puzzle elements per session. Components included patient history elements, PICO question formulation, research question development, evidence-searching strategies, critical appraisal indicators, evaluation of selected studies, and final evidence-informed clinical decision-making.
requirements: Printed card materials organized by EBM component category
Simulated clinical scenarios with shuffled component cards
Small-group collaborative work with facilitator feedback
constraints: Requires a trained facilitator with EBM expertise to provide structured formative feedback
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in clerkship rotations
target_learning_goals: sequential EBM decision-making pathway from question formulation to clinical decision-making
examples: Each group received four simulated clinical cases alongside shuffled cards representing different EBM components; students identified correct components and arranged them in sequence
key_sources: Zand Vahid, Bazi Ramin, Keshmiri Fatemeh. (2026). Game-based blended learning versus traditional lecture for evidence-based medicine (EBM) competencies in undergraduate medical students: a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09628-3

article_title: Puzzle-based pedagogic activity to address rote learning of antibiotic classes in clinical pharmacology course for undergraduate nursing students.
citation: Morén Constanza, Mariscal Emi Ruiz, Negredo Mónica, Preciado María, Martínez Gemma, Llaurado-Serra Mireia, Rosa Antonio, González Melinda, Rodríguez Natàlia, Martínez Laura. (2026). Puzzle-based pedagogic activity to address rote learning of antibiotic classes in clinical pharmacology course for undergraduate nursing students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09484-1
title: Constructivist, cognitive load, and Self-Determination Theory frameworks explain the Puzzle technique's pedagogical value
description: The authors interpret their findings through three educational theories. The Puzzle technique "aligns with constructivist principles, as students actively build knowledge through collaboration and peer teaching". Dividing complex pharmacological content into smaller segments "helps to reduce cognitive load, enhancing comprehension and retention". The intervention may also engage Self-Determination Theory dimensions by "fostering a sense of autonomy, competence, and social connection", enhancing intrinsic motivation.
requirements: Content must be divisible into manageable segments to reduce cognitive load
constraints: These frameworks are offered as interpretive lenses rather than directly tested mechanisms in this study
target_learning_goals: comprehension and retention of complex, memorization-intensive pharmacological content
key_sources: Morén Constanza, Mariscal Emi Ruiz, Negredo Mónica, Preciado María, Martínez Gemma, Llaurado-Serra Mireia, Rosa Antonio, González Melinda, Rodríguez Natàlia, Martínez Laura. (2026). article_title: Implementing peer-assisted learning in a dental flipped classroom: a model for postgraduate-undergraduate collaboration.
citation: Cui Ming-Wang, Zhang Miao-Miao, Dong Yu-Lei, Wen Tao, Xu Wei-Qi, Liu Qi-ZhiAng, Yang Ke-Zhen, Wang Zheng-Rou, Guo Zhu-Ling. (2026). Implementing peer-assisted learning in a dental flipped classroom: a model for postgraduate-undergraduate collaboration. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09315-3
title: PUC-FC: flipped classroom combined with postgraduate-undergraduate collaboration
description: The PUC-FC model is an advanced flipped-classroom paradigm in which senior postgraduates act as near-peer mentors across all course phases. Its "core concept is to use the clinical experience of senior postgraduates as scaffolding and digital technology as a lever" to address teacher shortage and delayed skill feedback. It constructs a "trinity educational ecology of 'knowledge transmission-skill training-experience inheritance'" through pre-class guidance, in-class one-on-one support and case debates, and post-class feedback reports within 48 hours.
requirements: Senior postgraduates with at least two years of clinical and academic experience, trained via a standardized mentoring protocol clarifying responsibilities, feedback standards, and intervention boundaries
constraints: The article notes total instructional exposure may confound results because the PUC-FC group received additional contact time through weekly online meetings and individualized mentoring
target_learning_goals: clinical operational competence
case analysis and clinical reasoning
learning satisfaction
examples: Five postgraduates guided 40 PUC-FC students, reducing the student-teacher ratio from 1:40 to 1:8
key_sources: Cui Ming-Wang, Zhang Miao-Miao, Dong Yu-Lei, Wen Tao, Xu Wei-Qi, Liu Qi-ZhiAng, Yang Ke-Zhen, Wang Zheng-Rou, Guo Zhu-Ling. (2026). Implementing peer-assisted learning in a dental flipped classroom: a model for postgraduate-undergraduate collaboration. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09315-3

article_title: Implementing peer-assisted learning in a dental flipped classroom: a model for postgraduate-undergraduate collaboration.
citation: Cui Ming-Wang, Zhang Miao-Miao, Dong Yu-Lei, Wen Tao, Xu Wei-Qi, Liu Qi-ZhiAng, Yang Ke-Zhen, Wang Zheng-Rou, Guo Zhu-Ling. (2026). Implementing peer-assisted learning in a dental flipped classroom: a model for postgraduate-undergraduate collaboration. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09315-3
title: Three-phase closed-loop flipped classroom workflow with near-peer mentoring
description: The model organizes instruction as a closed loop of pre-class, in-class, and post-class activities. Pre-class, students learn standardized 8–12 minute videos and submit preview notes and question lists with postgraduate guidance via weekly 30-minute online meetings. In-class, postgraduates give one-on-one real-time guidance during operation practice while teachers explain common difficulties and lead case debates. Post-class, postgraduates send targeted feedback reports and comment on reflection reports within 48 hours, forming "pre-class precise guidance-in-class in-depth interaction-post-class timely feedback".
requirements: Standardized pre-class video resources on an online teaching platform
Trained postgraduate teaching assistants
Structured feedback and reflection report workflow
target_learning_goals: clinical operational skills
clinical case analysis
reflective practice
examples: Students submitted preview notes and a list of 5 core questions before class; feedback reports were completed within 48 h after class
key_sources: Cui Ming-Wang, Zhang Miao-Miao, Dong Yu-Lei, Wen Tao, Xu Wei-Qi, Liu Qi-ZhiAng, Yang Ke-Zhen, Wang Zheng-Rou, Guo Zhu-Ling. (2026). Implementing peer-assisted learning in a dental flipped classroom: a model for postgraduate-undergraduate collaboration. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09315-3

article_title: Effects of game-based learning and flipped classroom strategies on performance and reasoning in patient safety education for surgical nursing students.
citation: Mehrdad M, Jambarsang S, Sadeghian H, Jabinian F, Keshmiri F. (2025). Effects of game-based learning and flipped classroom strategies on performance and reasoning in patient safety education for surgical nursing students. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0334545
title: Puzzle-based board game for surgical patient safety education addressing eight common patient safety risks
description: A puzzle board game designed around four elements of game-based pedagogy, played in small groups with rotating structured roles (e.g., scenario reader, solution proposer, checklist verifier), peer evaluation between groups, and facilitator feedback. "The educational puzzles were meticulously designed to address eight common patient safety risks", including the WHO safe surgery checklist stages, retained surgical items, medical gas cylinders, pathology samples, and pressure injuries. Gameplay involved classifying shuffled cards (e.g., into ISBAR handover structure) and completing a matrix game per puzzle step.
requirements: A trained facilitator team to monitor group dynamics and provide constructive feedback
Pre-class briefing materials (patient safety scripts and info-graphics) sent one week before sessions
constraints: Implemented monthly over four months in surgical nursing education at a single institution
target_learners: Surgical nursing students in six-month surgical unit internships
Practicing surgical nurses with six or more months of clinical experience
target_learning_goals: Reasoning skills in managing patient safety incidents
Performance in applying the WHO surgical safety checklist and related safety practices
examples: Groups classified puzzle cards into ISBAR, WHO safe surgery checklist, RSI prevention, medical gas, pathology sampling, and pressure injury categories, then completed matrix games and refined puzzles after peer evaluation
key_sources: Mehrdad M, Jambarsang S, Sadeghian H, Jabinian F, Keshmiri F. (2025). Effects of game-based learning and flipped classroom strategies on performance and reasoning in patient safety education for surgical nursing students. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0334545

article_title: Examining the Relationship Between Basic Nursing Skills, Hand Function, and Anxiety Levels in First-Year Nursing Students: A Correlational Study.
citation: Ela Yılmaz Coşkun, Aylin Yalçın Irmak, Merdiye Şendir. (2025). Examining the Relationship Between Basic Nursing Skills, Hand Function, and Anxiety Levels in First‐Year Nursing Students: A Correlational Study. Journal of Evaluation in Clinical Practice. https://doi.org/10.1111/jep.70191
title: Purdue Pegboard Test as an objective fine motor assessment for nursing student readiness
description: The Purdue Pegboard Test (Lafayette Instruments, model 3202) assesses fine motor skills by emphasising the speed and manipulative ability of the hands and fingers. In this study four subtests were administered — right hand, left hand, both hands, and assembly — with one-handed subtests counting pins inserted in 30 s and the assembly subtest counting pins with washers and clamping rings over 1 min. The authors describe it as providing "an objective means of assessing a student's readiness for skill‐intensive nursing procedures" and use it as the hand-function measure correlated with nursing skill checklists.
requirements: Administered per the user manual, in a room isolated from noise and crowds, with a trial run before scored subtests
constraints: The article notes use of a single hand function test may restrict the scope of the findings and recommends multiple validated measurement tools
target_learning_goals: fine motor dexterity relevant to clinical psychomotor nursing skills
examples: Four subtests (right hand, left hand, both hands, assembly) were administered to 123 first-year nursing students and correlated with basic nursing skill checklist scores
key_sources: Ela Yılmaz Coşkun, Aylin Yalçın Irmak, Merdiye Şendir. (2025). Examining the Relationship Between Basic Nursing Skills, Hand Function, and Anxiety Levels in First‐Year Nursing Students: A Correlational Study. article_title: The Use of Puzzles as a Teaching Technique in Nursing Education: A Randomized Controlled Study.
citation: Barış Eren Nadiye; Çiftçi Bahar. (2025). The Use of Puzzles as a Teaching Technique in Nursing Education: A Randomized Controlled Study. Journal of Evaluation in Clinical Practice. https://doi.org/10.1111/jep.70118
title: Puzzle booklet of ~20 puzzles on excretory activities used as post-lecture reinforcement
description: The researchers created 'A total of 200 questions on excretory activities' using wordmint.com, organized into 'Approximately 20 puzzles … each containing approximately 10 questions', printed as a booklet. It was distributed at the end of each lesson hour, collected, checked for mistakes, discussed individually with students, and returned for one week of repetition. Five faculty members evaluated its content and quality before use.
requirements: Students solve the puzzles after theoretical and laboratory instruction on the same topic
Faculty expert review of puzzle content and quality
Prevention of sharing between intervention and control groups
constraints: Evaluated only for the topic of excretory activities in a first-year fundamentals of nursing course
target_learning_goals: theoretical knowledge of excretory activities (urinary and intestinal elimination)
examples: Booklets containing 10 puzzle sheets were distributed at the end of each hour and collected at the end of the lesson, then returned for later repetition and collected after 1 week

article_title: Development and validation of a pudendal nerve block simulation-based educational intervention.
citation: Thiyagarajan D, Wheatley C, Salva CR, Lerner V, Saab SS. (2025). Development and validation of a pudendal nerve block simulation‐based educational intervention. Int J Gynecol Obstet. https://doi.org/10.1002/ijgo.70012
title: 35-minute simulation-based procedural training pattern: pre-evaluation, didactics, task-trainer practice with checklist assessment, and post-evaluation
description: A reusable session structure for teaching a low-frequency procedural skill: a preintervention survey and knowledge assessment, a didactic lecture covering history, anatomy, indications, procedural steps, and medication dosing and complications, hands-on task-trainer practice scored with a procedural checklist, and an identical post-intervention evaluation plus satisfaction items. The article specifies "Our final 35‐min intervention consists of (1) a 10‐min preintervention survey..." and reports significant pre/post gains with this structure.
requirements: A validated procedural checklist for objective assessment (maximum score 48 points)
A task trainer allowing practice and assessor verification of needle placement
Standardized answer key and grading system for scoring
constraints: Developed and refined through pilot testing and a Delphi expert panel recruited via snowball sampling, which the authors note limited the panel's expertise
target_learners: Residents and practicing clinicians in obstetrics, family medicine, and midwifery
target_learning_goals: Knowledge, comfort, and confidence in identifying candidates, discussing risks and benefits, offering and performing pudendal nerve block, and managing complications
examples: Implemented in multiple voluntary sessions at four academic institutions between July 2022 and February 2024, with participants who struggled given additional guided practice time
key_sources: Thiyagarajan D, Wheatley C, Salva CR, Lerner V, Saab SS. (2025). Development and validation of a pudendal nerve block simulation‐based educational intervention. Int J Gynecol Obstet. https://doi.org/10.1002/ijgo.70012

article_title: Development of a core competence model for improving medical college students' ability in respond to public health emergencies.
citation: Liu Fengqiong, Huang Shuqian, Chen Fa, Yang Suhua, Wu Lixin, Lin Yulan, He Baochang, Hu Zhijian. (2025). Development of a core competence model for improving medical college students’ ability in respond to public health emergencies. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1467832
title: A four-domain framework of 43 core competences for public health emergency response in medical students
description: The article develops a competence framework for public health emergency response education of public health majors, built via a two-round Delphi process with 21 experts in Fujian province. It contains 43 statements grouped into four domains: "intellectual competences, practical competences, behavioral competences, personnel and motivation". The intellectual domain covers knowledge such as epidemiology and laws; the practical domain covers outbreak investigation, information management and epidemic judgment; the behavioral domain covers professionalism, comprehensive quality and attitudes; the motivation domain covers innovation, learning and professional identity.
requirements: Competence statements must reach expert consensus, defined as a rating of 4 or 5 by over 80% of interviewees in Delphi scoring
constraints: The framework represents competence demands for the local government in Fujian province and was developed from a panel that cannot cover all emergency-related agencies, which the authors state may introduce selection bias
target_learners: undergraduate medical college students majoring in public health, preventive medicine, health inspection and quarantine, and public health administration
target_learning_goals: ability to respond to public health emergencies, including knowledge, practical skills, behavioral competences and motivation
examples: 21 experts from disease control centers, community health service centers and a medical university ranked 46 initial items on a five-point importance scale across two rounds; four low-consensus items were removed and leadership was added
key_sources: Liu Fengqiong, Huang Shuqian, Chen Fa, Yang Suhua, Wu Lixin, Lin Yulan, He Baochang, Hu Zhijian. (2025). Development of a core competence model for improving medical college students’ ability in respond to public health emergencies. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2025.1467832

article_title: Enhancing puncture skills training with generative AI and digital technologies: a parallel cohort study.
citation: Ji Zhe, Jiang Yuliang, Sun Haitao, Qiu Bin, Chen Yi, Li Mao, Fan Jinghong, Wang Junjie. (2024). Enhancing puncture skills training with generative AI and digital technologies: a parallel cohort study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06217-0
title: Universal 3D-printed puncture template with adjustable navigation frame plus BTPS imaging software as a digital puncture-training apparatus
description: The training apparatus combines two digital components. First, "universally applicable coplanar templates capable of mass production for puncture practices" with guiding holes spaced at 2.5 mm intervals, mounted on a multi-joint navigation frame adjustable to any angle, guiding the needle toward the imaging target. Second, the BTPS planning system developed by Beihang University provides multimodal image fusion, three-dimensional reconstruction, needle-track planning, and quantitative measurements such as needle depth, angle, and proximity to vital structures. Group 2 trained with both; Group 3 added ChatGPT.
requirements: Requires the template affixed to a versatile navigation frame with articulating joints for angle adjustment, and access to the BTPS planning system with CT/MRI data
constraints: The templates are standardized tools, not individualized 3D-printed models of specific patients
target_learners: Refresher doctors training in CT-guided puncture procedures
target_learning_goals: Accurate needle trajectory alignment and mastery of CT-guided puncture techniques
examples: Group 2 (n = 30) trained with the template and BTPS alongside conventional lectures, reading, observation, and supervised practice, achieving post-training skill scores of 4.0 ± 0.18
key_sources: Ji Zhe, Jiang Yuliang, Sun Haitao, Qiu Bin, Chen Yi, Li Mao, Fan Jinghong, Wang Junjie. (2024). Enhancing puncture skills training with generative AI and digital technologies: a parallel cohort study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06217-0

article_title: Biomedical students' self-efficacy and academic performance by gender in a flipped learning haematology course.
citation: Algarni Abdulrahman Abdulrahman. (2024). Biomedical students’ self-efficacy and academic performance by gender in a flipped learning haematology course. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05421-2
title: When flipping a course, design purposeful in-person activities rather than simply exporting pre-class content online
description: The article concludes that pre-class video content alone does not capture the flipped classroom's value; educators should pair out-of-class content with structured in-class active learning. In its conclusions the article warns that "simply exporting pre-class content without intention toward purposeful in-person activities risks losing existing benefits of face-to-face education". The study's own design illustrates the principle: in-class time was used for group problem-solving, case-scenario debates, and instructor feedback, enabled by students having already engaged with online materials.
requirements: Students must engage with pre-class online materials so in-class time can be devoted to active participation rather than lecturing
constraints: The article states more research is needed into optimal configurations of pre-class and in-class activities to potentiate knowledge gains
target_learners: Health professions students, including medical undergraduates
target_learning_goals: Knowledge application and problem-solving during class time, plus affective outcomes such as self-efficacy
examples: The intervention group's in-class sessions replaced lecture time with student-led discourse, group allocation, handouts of problem-solving inquiries and case scenarios, and a whole-class debate on clinical scenarios
key_sources: Algarni Abdulrahman Abdulrahman. (2024). Biomedical students’ self-efficacy and academic performance by gender in a flipped learning haematology course. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05421-2

article_title: The first OSCE; does students' experience of performing in public affect their results?
citation: Chan Michael, Bax Nigel, Woodley Caroline, Jennings Michael, Nicolson Rod, Chan Philip. (2015). The first OSCE; does students’ experience of performing in public affect their results? BMC Medical Education, 15, 59. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-015-0343-0
title: 0–3 coding framework for public performance experience in medical school admission statements
description: A coding scheme applied to UCAS personal statements to quantify pre-admission public performance experience across vocal and instrumental music, theatre, dance, sport, and debate/public speaking. "Participation in each activity was scored 0–3, where 0 was no record, 1 = leisure time activity, 2 = activity at school or local level, 3 = activity at district, regional or national level." Activities were grouped into verbal (vocal music, theatre, debate) and motor (sport, instrumental music, dance) composites, with scores summed within groups. Coding was developed with senior staff agreement and applied by a single coder with consistency checks.
requirements: Access to applicants' original admission statements in individual student files, coded by a researcher independent of the institution as required by the ethics committee
constraints: Statements cannot be directly verified, and students may not have declared activities fully or may have developed new activities in the intervening years
target_learning_goals: predicting clinical examination performance from pre-admission personal qualities
examples: The framework was applied to the whole 265-student cohort's statements, yielding total scores ranging from 0 to 15 against a maximum possible of 18
key_sources: Chan Michael, Bax Nigel, Woodley Caroline, Jennings Michael, Nicolson Rod, Chan Philip. (2015). The first OSCE; does students’ experience of performing in public affect their results? BMC Medical Education, 15, 59. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-015-0343-0
